## TL;DR

- Customizing an agent means giving it the context and tools it needs, and building checks on its work. In my experience, teams put far more into the first.
- Off-the-shelf agents make people faster, but the business gains only when the work is redesigned around them.
- Build your own agent when it should run part of a process rather than assist one person. How much of the process to hand it depends on how bad an uncaught mistake could get, and who answers for it.
- Own the model when harness changes hit diminishing returns and frontier model APIs still fail your task, cost too much at your volume, or your data cannot leave your walls.
- Build an eval from your own tasks. It tells you when to move a layer deeper, and it outlasts every model and harness around it.

Agents keep making the news. In September 2025, MIT's CRESt [found a better fuel-cell catalyst](https://news.mit.edu/2025/ai-system-learns-many-types-scientific-information-and-runs-experiments-discovering-new-materials-0925) after more than 900 experiments, and this September about 10,000 of OpenAI's agents [settled the Navier–Stokes problem](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-has-solved-one-of-maths-1-million-millennium-prize-problems-20260908/), one of the Millennium Prize problems. Then you try an agent in your day-to-day work, and it does not work nearly as well. It keeps needing you to steer it, and it tends to say it is done when it is not.

Why the difference? Part of it is the model and the compute behind it. The rest is that both problems sit in verifiable domains, and each agent ran inside a system built around its verifier: robots made and tested the catalysts CRESt proposed, and a proof checker, Lean, confirmed every step of the proof OpenAI's agents wrote. Most business work is not like that. No program can tell you whether a contract summary left out the clause that matters, or whether a support reply actually solved the customer's problem.

So you may need a lot of customization before an agent works reliably for you. You need to give it the context and tools it needs. You also need to build automated verification where the work allows, and leave the rest of the verification to people.

But which customizations pay off for you? When should you stop buying and start building your own agents or models? To answer, I need a few terms first.

Described by what it does, an agent [runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/18/agents/): it plans a step, acts, looks at the result, and changes course when something fails. Described by what it is made of, an agent is [model + harness](https://www.langchain.com/blog/the-anatomy-of-an-agent-harness). The harness is everything around the model: the instructions and context, its tools, the workflow that coordinates its steps, and the checks that catch its mistakes. The agent acts on an environment: the systems and data it works in, such as a codebase, a CRM or an outside API.

With those terms, I sort the options into three layers, from the outside in: connecting an off-the-shelf agent to your data and tools, building your own agent on a frontier model, and owning the model. It usually makes sense to take them in that order. Buy an off-the-shelf agent first, build your own when you want it to run part of a process rather than help one person, and train a model when harness changes hit diminishing returns. An eval built from your own tasks is how you tell when to move. The diagram and table below summarize the three layers.

![](fig-layers-rings.svg){fig-alt="Three nested rings: integration and adoption on the outside, the harness in the middle, the model at the core. Each layer you own takes you closer to the model."}

| Layer | Business value | Bottleneck |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Integration and adoption | People working faster | How many people you have |
| 2. Harness engineering | Agent work built into your process | How much work you decide to automate |
| 3. Model engineering | Control, cost or a capability others cannot rent | How long until frontier models match it |

![](fig-layer-products.svg){fig-alt="Off-the-shelf products at each layer, as of October 2026: vendor agents and workplace agents at layer 1; models, frameworks, agent SDKs, open-source agents and hosting platforms at layer 2; open weights, data labeling firms, managed training services and GPUs at layer 3."}

Each layer pays off in a different way. An off-the-shelf agent raises individual productivity, so the return grows with your headcount. Your own agent can automate part of a process end to end, so the return grows with the volume of that work. Your own model can give you what a rented one cannot: a capability, a lower unit cost, or full control of your data. Most of that lasts only until frontier models catch up. An advantage built on your own data can last much longer on your own tasks, because frontier models are not trained on it.

## Layer 1: integration and adoption

![](fig-layer1-parts.svg){fig-alt="Layer 1, the outer ring, has four parts: integrations and knowledge, instruction files and skills, review and governance, and adoption and change management."}

### Connecting data, tools and knowledge

Integration is a good place to start. You take an off-the-shelf agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, connect it to your data, set what it may do, and change how your people work. In practice, this means you can build an MCP server that lets Claude read and update your ticketing system, write an AGENTS.md file that tells the agent how your code is built and tested, package your brand guidelines as a skill the agent loads when it makes slides, and define permission rules that let it run tests but never touch production. Put access rules close to the tools, not in the agent's instructions, which a model can ignore. Rules about the agent's own actions, such as which shell commands it may run, go in a hook that checks each call before it runs. Rules about a business system go in its server: a refund tool that refuses amounts over $500, or files them for a manager to approve, enforces that rule for every agent that calls it, including ones you build later.

MCP has become the usual way to connect an agent to a company's tools and data, and inside companies it tends to become shared infrastructure. Stripe's internal Toolshed holds ["nearly 500 MCP tools"](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2) that many agents use, from its coding agents to Slack bots. LinkedIn pairs its MCP servers with playbooks, step-by-step workflows written by its engineers that agents can call like tools. Given a customer-issue ticket, one playbook pulls the relevant logs, finds similar past incidents, points to the likely code and writes its findings back into the ticket, and LinkedIn reports [initial triage time down about 70%](https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/ai/contextual-agent-playbooks-and-tools-how-linkedin-gave-ai-coding-agents-organizational-context). Once many teams publish servers, someone has to decide which ones agents may reach. Pinterest lets only servers in a [central registry](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/04/pinterest-mcp-ecosystem) run in production, and each must pass security, legal and privacy review before it is listed.

MCP's known weakness is scale. Uber runs more than a thousand MCP servers behind a gateway, and loading every tool description cost tens of thousands of tokens a session. Agents now work around this themselves: Claude Code [loads MCP tool descriptions only when a task needs them](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), by default. The largest users go further. [Uber](https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/efficient-software-factory/) and [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/internal-ai-engineering-stack/) keep their MCP servers but hide the tool list. Uber turned its gateway's 1,000-plus tools into shell commands that call the gateway only when run, and Cloudflare's portal shows the agent just two tools, search and execute, so it writes code to reach the rest.

Once connected, an agent still needs the company's knowledge, which lives in documents, wikis, tickets and chat history. Off-the-shelf agents mostly fetch it themselves, through connectors or by searching files, rather than through a retrieval pipeline you build. Claude Code loads its instruction files up front and then uses search tools to ["retrieve files just-in-time"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), which Anthropic says avoids stale indexes. Finding the right document in raw company data is still hard. In a synthetic company of 500,000 Slack messages, emails, tickets and documents, the best of three methods [answered 68.8% of questions correctly](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05253). It was plain keyword search, ahead of an agent with shell tools at 60.6% and vector search at 51.4%. Organizing the knowledge first helps. Vercel cut its data agent down to plain file access, and it worked only ["because our semantic layer was already good documentation."](https://vercel.com/blog/we-removed-80-percent-of-our-agents-tools) Andrej Karpathy's [LLM wiki](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) has an agent turn raw documents into linked pages that it keeps current. Someone has to own that content, because it goes stale like the instruction files below.

### Instruction files and skills

Instruction files and skills tell the agent how your team works, and whether they help depends on what is in them. Cloudflare [generated AGENTS.md files for about 3,900 repositories](https://blog.cloudflare.com/internal-ai-engineering-stack/), and Intercom [runs a weekly job that fact-checks every CLAUDE.md](https://ideas.fin.ai/p/how-we-use-claude-code-today-at-intercom). Vercel's compressed docs index took its agent from 53% to [100% on its own evals](https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals). In 56% of cases the agent never invoked its Next.js skill, which added nothing unless the agent was told to use it. An instruction file is always loaded; a skill is loaded only when the agent decides the task needs one. The skill's short description decides when the agent uses it. Anthropic tuned the descriptions of its own document skills, and [triggering improved for 5 of 6](https://claude.com/blog/improving-skill-creator-test-measure-and-refine-agent-skills). An ETH Zurich study found context files [did not generally improve success](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988) and raised cost, though the agents followed the instructions they were given and the authors found the files useful for non-standard coding practices. They help most when they hold what the model cannot guess, such as your conventions and internal APIs.

Even useful instruction files and skills go stale, in two ways. Code changes under them, and in a study of thousands of context files, teams [mostly added instructions and rarely deleted any](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12884). Models change too. Anthropic's guide for Fable 5 says ["Skills developed for prior models are often too prescriptive"](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5) and can degrade output, and OpenAI writes that with GPT-6 Astra, ["overly specific guidance can now hinder results"](https://developers.openai.com/blog/rethinking-skills-and-prompts-for-gpt-6-astra). Newer models need less hand-holding, and instructions written for older ones can get in their way. Memory goes stale the same way. Anthropic tells Cowork users that skills and memory files written for an earlier model ["often carry corrections that model needed"](https://claude.com/blog/working-with-claude-fable-5-in-claude-cowork), which can constrain a new one. Not all skills fade the same way. Anthropic writes that skills that help a model do what it cannot yet do reliably ["may become less necessary as models improve"](https://claude.com/blog/improving-skill-creator-test-measure-and-refine-agent-skills), while skills that encode your team's own process are more durable. So treat these files like code: keep a few small tests that show they still help, and rerun them when you change models.

### Review and governance

The more code agents write, the more people have to review. Across 22,000 developers in 2026, Faros found [median review time up fivefold](https://www.faros.ai/research/ai-acceleration-whiplash). Spotify reports a sharp rise in pull requests and, with it, ["76% more PRs to review"](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2026/6/code-with-claude-coding-is-no-longer-the-constraint). Its answer is ["auto-merging what's safe, focusing review where it matters most"](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2026/6/code-with-claude-coding-is-no-longer-the-constraint). How it decides what is safe comes up again in layer 2. Many teams add an AI reviewer to CI, or an LLM judge that scores output against a rubric, and either helps as a first pass. Anthropic says its AI reviewer raised the share of pull requests getting substantive comments [from 16% to 54%](https://claude.com/blog/code-review). Cloudflare's AI reviewer costs about a dollar a review, and the company says it ["isn't a replacement for human code review, at least not yet"](https://blog.cloudflare.com/ai-code-review/). Independent studies are less flattering. Developers adopt AI review suggestions [less often](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15911) than human ones, and on 2026 benchmarks AI reviewers catch roughly [15 to 31%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26130) of the issues human reviewers flag. I found no controlled study showing that AI review reduces the bugs that reach production.

Then comes governing the agent, which means deciding what it may do, what it may spend and who answers for it. On the technical side, Intercom uses a [permission hook](https://ideas.fin.ai/p/how-we-use-claude-code-today-at-intercom) that sorts the agent's shell commands into green, yellow and red, with rules drawn from two weeks of session transcripts. On cost, Uber shows engineers a [live cost counter](https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/efficient-software-factory/), alerts them at 50%, 80% and 100% of expected spend, and defaults reasoning effort to medium. Weekly users grew sevenfold while its total AI spend "relatively stabilized". The organizational part is the hardest to measure, and model benchmarks say nothing about it: who may use which agent on which data, what needs sign-off, and how incidents get reported. My team at KUNGFU.AI calls this [human-machine teaming](https://www.kungfu.ai/human-machine-teaming). Regulation is heading the same way. The EU AI Act's [Article 14](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/14/) requires that a person can oversee, override and stop high-risk systems, with obligations phasing in from December 2027.

### Turning use into business gains

For technical leaders, getting people to use agents is one problem and turning that use into business gains is another. In Microsoft's early 2026 rollout of Claude Code and Copilot CLI, use [spread mainly from peer to peer](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.01418), and users merged about 24% more pull requests. Yet across more than 400 companies, DX found AI usage up 65% while median pull-request throughput rose only [7.76%](https://getdx.com/report/ai-and-engineering-velocity-a-longitudinal-analysis/), and in a survey of nearly 6,000 executives, [89% reported no impact on labor productivity](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34836). My reading is that two things keep the gains from being realized. First, the work moves downstream: faster coding feeds review, testing and deployment, which did not speed up. In the Faros data, developers completed more tasks, but there were [more incidents per pull request and fewer deployments a week](https://www.faros.ai/research/ai-acceleration-whiplash). Second, saved time adds nothing unless someone puts it to other use. If nobody plans what the freed hours are for, a task done faster changes nothing the business can see. That fits [McKinsey's survey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai), where redesigning how the work gets done was more closely tied to profit from AI than anything else it measured, technology included.

That survey shows a correlation. A [2026 trial of 515 startups](https://sites.insead.edu/facultyresearch/research/doc.cfm?did=75343) tested cause and effect. All had the same AI tools, and some, picked at random, were also shown how other firms had reorganized their work around AI. Those firms found 44% more uses for AI, completed 12% more tasks and earned 1.9 times the revenue, and their demand for staff did not change. The authors conclude that "discovering where and how to deploy AI is a key bottleneck". These were early-stage startups in a three-month program, so the numbers may not carry over to a large company. A [2026 study of accountants](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/human-ai-accounting-early-evidence-field) shows what the change can look like. On an AI accounting platform serving 79 small and mid-sized firms, AI use went with a shift in effort from routine data entry to business communication and quality assurance, and with books that closed faster at month end. Accountants stepped in mainly when the AI's confidence score was low. The study is observational, so it shows an association, not a cause.

An education company in a [2026 Stanford study of 51 AI deployments](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2026/03/EnterpriseAIPlaybook_PereiraGraylinBrynjolfsson.pdf) changed the work in two ways. Its subject experts now review AI drafts of course material instead of writing it, which the company says saved millions. Its engineers saved 20 to 30% of their time with coding assistants, and the company spent that time on its product backlog instead of cutting staff.

As companies get more out of agents, some outgrow off-the-shelf ones and build their own on top of the integration work they have already done.

## Layer 2: harness engineering

![](fig-layer2-parts.svg){fig-alt="Layer 2, the middle ring, has five parts: context engineering, tools and access, orchestration, model routing, and evals."}

An off-the-shelf agent makes each person faster. To automate a whole process, companies have built their own agent and redesigned the work around it. Stripe's engineers still [work with agents such as Claude and Cursor](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents), but Stripe built its own for unattended work, because off-the-shelf local coding agents are ["optimized for working through code changes as a companion to engineers"](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2). A typical run ["starts in a Slack message and ends in a pull request which passes CI"](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents), and a person reviews it before it merges. Stripe now merges more than 1,300 of these pull requests a week, none containing human-written code. Ramp's agent, Inspect, writes about [30% of merged pull requests](https://builders.ramp.com/post/why-we-built-our-background-agent) in its frontend and backend repositories.

Claude Code and Codex can already run without a person, with [permission rules, sandboxes and admin policies](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions) ([Codex's equivalents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-approvals-security)). What you still need to do is route questions to the right person, scope credentials to each run, and hard-code the steps that must never vary. Neither company wrote the agent loop from scratch. Stripe [forked the open-source agent goose](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2) in late 2024, then added a cloud development machine for each run, workflows that mix fixed steps such as running linters and pushing code with agent steps, and nearly 500 tools that reach its internal systems. Ramp [recommends building on](https://builders.ramp.com/post/why-we-built-our-background-agent) the open-source agent OpenCode. It runs each session in a sandboxed virtual machine on Modal, connects the agent to Sentry, Datadog, GitHub, Slack and other systems, and lets people start a session from Slack, a web app, a Chrome extension or VS Code. I found no published head-to-head of an in-house agent against an off-the-shelf one on the same work, so these are the builders' own accounts.

Company data raises the same problems. With a person at the keyboard, Claude Code connected to a warehouse or CRM can act with that person's credentials, and they read each answer. Unattended, it needs credentials of its own, typically a service account that often sees more than any one employee, and its [permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions) stop at the tool name: you can allow a query tool, but not limit it to reading three tables. Those limits have to sit in the system around the agent: database roles scoped to whoever made the request, writes through your own APIs rather than raw SQL, business definitions and evals so that "active customer" means what finance means, and a decision about which data may be sent to the model at all.

Owning the agent gives you control of the five parts in the figure above: what the agent sees at each step and what it remembers across sessions (context engineering), which tools it has and what they can reach, as whom (tools and access), what happens between model calls (orchestration), which model handles each step (model routing), and how you know it works (evals). Changing the harness alone can move results a lot: LangChain gained 14 points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, from 52.8% to 66.5%, by [changing only the harness](https://www.langchain.com/blog/improving-deep-agents-with-harness-engineering) around a fixed model. Stripe customized its coding agents to control the first three. Each gets context scoped to the files it is working in and ["an intentionally small subset of tools"](https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2), and runs inside a workflow where steps such as "Run configured linters" and "Push changes" "don't invoke an LLM at all." Stripe says that saves tokens and gives the agent "a little less opportunity to get things wrong." Harvey customized its legal agents, which handle work such as reviewing a data room, to control the fourth. It built its own runtime so they can run ["on essentially any model"](https://www.harvey.ai/blog/why-we-built-our-own-cloud-agent-infrastructure) under zero data retention, and reports "3-5x cost reductions versus a frontier-only approach."

What limits this layer is how much of the work you can hand the agent. Deciding that, along with what starts a run and where a person reviews, redesigns the process, and it is a business decision as much as a technical one. It depends on how bad an uncaught mistake could get, and on who answers for it. The rest of this part covers how to build the agent and when to split it across several, then how it fails, how to prevent failures by giving the agent what it needs, how to catch them with checks, and finally how to decide what to hand over.

### Building it

I see three main ways to build your own harness: on a framework such as LangGraph, on an existing agent such as the open-source OpenCode, or directly with the model's API. Each gives you a different head start and a different maintenance burden. Frameworks and hand-written loops are both common in production. In [one study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04123), 17 of 20 deployed teams it interviewed wrote their own loop on direct API calls, while in the same paper's survey of practitioners, 61% used a framework, LangChain or LangGraph most often. Even OpenAI's own SDK documentation says to use the raw API ["when you want to own the loop"](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/).

With a framework or an existing agent, you also follow releases you do not control. Whichever path you take, you retune the harness when models change, because it is built around one model's habits. Vercel found that ["every model update meant re-calibrating our constraints"](https://vercel.com/blog/we-removed-80-percent-of-our-agents-tools), and Anthropic added context resets to work around one model's habit of wrapping up early, only to find on the next model that they ["had become dead weight"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents).

My advice is to start simple and be eval-driven. Pick whatever gets you to a working eval fastest, even if you expect to outgrow it, and change it only when the eval shows it is holding you back. Without an eval, you may not notice when a feature you switch on makes your agent worse. In one 2026 study, turning on CrewAI's optional planning step, which asks the model to write its plan in a fixed format, cut a small open model's accuracy on math problems [from 80% to 48%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03128), because the model often broke the format. On the strongest model tested, the same step barely changed accuracy but still added overhead.

### When to go multi-agent

If you followed agent news this year, much of it was about teams of agents. In January, Cursor had [hundreds of agents](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents) build a web browser from scratch over about a week. In February, Anthropic had [16 agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler) write a C compiler. In September, [about 10,000 OpenAI agents](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-has-solved-one-of-maths-1-million-millennium-prize-problems-20260908/) produced the Navier–Stokes proof. Should your agent be a team too?

First, the benefits. A multi-agent system helps in two ways: it divides the work among agents, and it gives agents specialized roles. Dividing the work gives each agent a clean context, which matters because models get less reliable as their context fills, an effect known as context rot. In one 2026 study, frontier models acting as monitors missed a dangerous action [2 to 30 times more often](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12366) when it came after 800,000 tokens of harmless activity than when it appeared on its own. A subagent can read many files and hand back a short summary, so the main agent never sees the clutter. When the parts are independent, they can also run at once, which makes work faster and makes room for work too big for one agent. Moonshot reports its Kimi swarm reached its target [3 to 4.5 times faster](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02276) than a single agent on a wide search task, and Cursor's hundreds of agents wrote [over a million lines of code](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents) for its browser. Results can improve too: Google found gains of [up to 80.8%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296) on financial analysis, a task that splits cleanly, even with compute held equal. Specialized roles, such as a planner, workers and a reviewer, give each agent a narrower job and its own tools, which Anthropic lists among the cases where [multi-agent systems win](https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them). A reviewer role is a common addition (the generator–verifier pattern), though the evidence for it is mixed. I will talk more about it in a later section about catching failures.

Now the downsides. A multi-agent system often costs more for no gain, and sometimes does worse, especially when the work does not split cleanly or one agent already does the task well. Across Google's 260 setups, the effect averaged about zero and fell as low as [−70.0% on sequential planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296), and once a single agent scored above about 45%, adding agents hurt. On one benchmark, most of the gain came from context management that one agent can do itself: Moonshot reports its swarm scored 78.4% on BrowseComp against 60.6% for a single agent, but a single agent that simply discarded old context reached [74.9%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02276). Anthropic warns that teams have spent months on multi-agent designs ["only to discover that improved prompting on a single agent achieved equivalent results"](https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them). And even when it works, extra agents often make work faster but more expensive. OpenAI's Noam Brown says four agents finish [about twice as fast](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/noam-brown), so "you're paying 2x more," and how much faster "does depend a lot on the problem."

![Data: Kim et al., Google, "Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems", arXiv 2512.08296 v3 (April 2026), Figure 2 and Section 4. Each bar spans the worst to best multi-agent design on that benchmark, at matched compute. Redrawn from the published numbers.](fig-multiagent-range.svg){fig-alt="Range of change against a single agent across multi-agent designs on six benchmarks: from +57% to +80.8% on financial analysis down to −70% to −39.1% on sequential planning."}

If you do split the work among multiple agents, have a clear responsibility about who may change what. Agents that edit the same file or data collide, as threads do in concurrent programming. A good setup is to have one agent write while the others read, review or advise: Cognition, which wrote "Don't Build Multi-Agents" in 2025, now runs setups where ["multiple agents contribute intelligence to a task while writes stay single-threaded"](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working). Where several agents must write, give each a self-contained task; Anthropic recommends ["starting with orchestrator-subagent"](https://claude.com/blog/multi-agent-coordination-patterns) for most uses. Without that structure, agents collide. In CooperBench, where each agent built a feature touching the same code, success fell from 68.6% with two agents to [30.0% with four](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13295). Cursor tried locks, then optimistic concurrency, and still found that twenty peer agents ["would slow down to the effective throughput of two or three"](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents). A planner with workers fixed most of it. Agents also fail in ways threads do not: without a hierarchy, Cursor's agents ["became risk-averse"](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents) and avoided hard tasks.

Then check the work, as mechanically as you can. The compiler and the Navier–Stokes proof above both had deterministic verifiers. The compiler's agents were judged by test suites, a continuous-integration gate and GCC as a known-good reference, and its author writes that the task verifier must be ["nearly perfect"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler), otherwise Claude will solve the wrong problem. The proof was [checked in Lean](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-has-solved-one-of-maths-1-million-millennium-prize-problems-20260908/), a proof assistant, though people must still confirm that the Lean statement says what mathematicians meant. Most business work has no deterministic verifier. A verifier agent is the usual substitute, but the evidence for it is thin and conditional: it helps when it is at least as capable as the agent it checks and has explicit criteria, and a weaker reviewer can make results worse (see Catching failures). Given only a generic instruction, such as checking whether the output is good, it ["will rubber-stamp the generator's output"](https://claude.com/blog/multi-agent-coordination-patterns). For code, Anthropic's example is a verifier that writes and runs tests, which brings back a deterministic check. Models also [share blind spots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962): in a study of more than 350 models, when two models both got a question wrong on one benchmark, they gave the same wrong answer 60% of the time. Where a missed mistake would be costly, a person should look.

Letting agents organize themselves is the newest direction, and the results split on model strength. Given only a mission and a fixed turn order, strong models invented their own roles and [beat a central coordinator by 14%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28990), while weaker models still needed rigid structure. But self-organized teams tend to average opinions rather than defer to the expert among them, and [did worse than their best member](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01011) even when told who the expert was. Automatically designed multi-agent systems lost to one model voting over several samples, at [up to ten times the cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13003). Agents also organize themselves when nobody asked them to, and the Hugging Face incident below is the clearest case.

### How it fails

To make an agent reliable in real work, you first need to know when and how it fails. Reliability here means more than success rate: an agent that solves a task most of the time may still give a different answer on the next run, break when the input changes slightly, or fail without warning. Better models have raised success rates but barely improved reliability. Across 15 models up to GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7, capability gains ["have only yielded small improvements in reliability"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16666). The newest models still vary from run to run. An October 2026 study asked eight frontier models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8, to sort the same customer feedback into themes several times. Even the most stable model, Fable 5, changed [about 60% of its themes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08036) from one run to the next. With Claude Opus 4.8, giving the agent a stored list of themes to sort into, rather than inventing them on each run, cut the change from about three themes in four to one in ten. Where an answer should stay the same from run to run, fix the set of possible answers and store each decision rather than regenerate it.

An agent can also fail by costing too much. Some of that is simply the price of frontier models. In my document-extraction work, a legal document often takes 8,000 to 10,000 tokens to read, and long ones take more. At [list prices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing), one read of a 10,000-token document with a 2,000-token answer costs about $0.08 on Claude Opus 5.5, $0.04 on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and $0.002 on Claude Haiku 5.5. At 5 million documents a year, that is $400,000, $200,000 and $10,000, before retries and review steps multiply it.

### Preventing failures

Most failed runs start with the agent working from a wrong or incomplete picture of the task, not from an inability to do the work. Zhao and colleagues traced the [decisive mistake](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09510) in more than a thousand failed terminal-agent runs. In 58% of them the agent had the information it needed, or could have checked it, and did not use it. The largest single cause was acting on an assumption it never checked, followed by dropping a requirement it had been given. About a quarter lacked knowledge of a tool or domain, and fewer than one in ten had a sound plan and carried it out badly. The decisive mistake came early, around the seventh step. The agents were 2025 models, so the proportions will shift, but the shape matches what I have seen.

Better models may avoid many of these mistakes. What the harness can do is leave the agent less to work out for itself. Some of this works with an off-the-shelf agent too, through instruction files and skills. Give the agent the facts it cannot know, and keep them short. In [SkillsBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12670), short curated skills helped, comprehensive documentation barely moved the score, and skills a model wrote for itself did worse than none. Make asking a separate step. A check for "is this underspecified?" recovered most of what Claude Sonnet 4.5 lost when task details were hidden, [from 54.8% back to 69.4%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26233). Asking helps less when the gap only shows up mid-task, which is the normal case; even with a tool for asking a person, Claude Opus 4.6 fell from 90.7% to [39.3% on SQL tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.09408) once it had to decide for itself when to ask. And give the agent room to look before it acts. Agents that explore longer before their first edit [succeed more often](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02547), and plans written by people after the agent explored [more than tripled](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14337) Claude Code's success on long tasks.

The cheapest wins I have had came from deciding what goes into each call. In a document extraction pipeline, the target schema was the largest thing in the prompt, so we compacted it before each call. Tokens on those calls fell by about two thirds, and field-level agreement with the full schema held at 97%. My colleague Matt Kilpatrick built compaction into the agent loop itself, keeping a short list of facts, a running summary, the last few turns and shortened tool results. On a long-context search task, his agent used about 40% fewer tokens than the same agent with off-the-shelf memory libraries, and every run passed the task's checks.

Long-term memory can help a lot, but only while it stays current. Databricks gave a data agent memories drawn from 62 records of past user conversations, filtered by an LLM judge, and its accuracy [rose from 2.5% to over 50%](https://www.databricks.com/blog/memory-scaling-ai-agents), past a baseline curated by experts. How that knowledge is organized matters too. Before each task, Harvey had an agent build a graph of the parties, dates and contract versions in a client matter, and [reports](https://www.harvey.ai/blog/improving-agent-accuracy-with-harvey-graph) rubric pass rates up to 30% higher at up to half the cost on its own legal benchmark. Keeping it current is the hard part. A 2026 survey of agent harnesses puts it generally: agents ["often fail not because no state is stored, but because the wrong state is preserved, the right state cannot be retrieved, or stale state is treated as current"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20683). In [STALE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06527), a 2026 benchmark where a later fact quietly overturns an earlier one, the best model got 55.2% right overall, most dedicated memory frameworks scored below 10%, and models "often accept outdated assumptions embedded in a user's query." Memory can also be attacked. Microsoft's red team found that poisoning an agent's memory [takes a single successful injection](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/04/updating-taxonomy-failure-modes-agentic-ai-systems-year-red-teaming-taught-us/), which the agent then carries into later sessions. Whether you turn on a product's memory or build your own, test it like an instruction file, including what it does when a fact changes.

Which tools to give depends on the model. Strong models do best with the shell and file tools they were trained on. With Opus 4.8, bash alone scored 69.4% on TheAgentCompany against 44.9% with a catalog of typed tools, at [a third of the cost per task](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11999). Smaller models behave differently. With only a shell, NVIDIA's 30B Nemotron kept calling tools it had been trained on that did not exist, which ended 66% of its runs, and predefined tools raised its success [from 10.2% to 25.2%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20804). Either way, match the tool schemas the model was trained on. A cheaper model with more tools is a fair experiment when cost matters, but I have not found a study where one matched a frontier model, so measure it on your own task.

Unattended agents are easy to manipulate. In one test, agents [obeyed most requests from people who were not their owner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20021), leaking 124 email records. Limits built into the system prevent much of this: sandboxes, least privilege, allowlists, human approval, and designs that keep untrusted data away from instructions. Keep credentials out of the sandbox where the agent's code runs. OpenAI runs the harness apart from that sandbox because it ["helps keep credentials out of environments where model-generated code executes"](https://openai.com/index/the-next-evolution-of-the-agents-sdk/). These limits fail too. Microsoft's red team found getting around human approval ["the most consistently exploited failure mode"](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/04/updating-taxonomy-failure-modes-agentic-ai-systems-year-red-teaming-taught-us/).

### Catching failures

The worst failures are the ones where the agent reports success. In one study of failed coding-agent runs, a quarter [claimed success with fake evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09510), which the authors call "a consequence of failure rather than its source." Anthropic's [Opus 4.8 system card](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/0b4915911bb0d19eca5b5ee635c80fef830a37ea.pdf) describes Claude telling a researcher "I verified this myself" about a model name that a subagent had only guessed; the researcher found out by asking a colleague. The same pattern shows up in court. In [Lnu v. Blanche](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2026/06/03/24-4790.pdf), a brief cited two cases that do not exist, and the Ninth Circuit noted that "the Attorney General did not flag the fabricated citations." One of the petitioners' own lawyers caught them while preparing for oral argument. A KPMG report on agentic AI got [most of its citations wrong](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/06/12/kpmgs-ai-report-turns-into-a-demo-of-ai-hallucinations/5255029), and an outside group found it eight months after publication. In the one longitudinal study of a production agent runtime, silent failures took [up to 60 days](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14589) to surface, most were found by people rather than tests, and 87% could have been blocked by regression tests written afterwards. Turn each silent failure you catch into a test.

Judge whether a run is stuck or finished from evidence, not from the agent's own account. Loop detectors and step budgets fire after the decisive mistake, so use them to escalate rather than to prevent. Check the claimed result itself: run the tests, open the output, compare it with what the task asked for. Check requirements with something other than the agent, because models [restate a constraint while breaking it](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28031).

Checking with something other than the agent is also the strongest case for a second agent, as a checker. Its independence comes from what it checks against and how capable it is, not from running on a different model. Shopify's security harness has a verifier on a different model write and run tests against each finding. In one audit, [every one of 30-plus candidate vulnerabilities](https://shopify.engineering/building-an-agentic-harness-that-outlasts-the-model) was downgraded, found to be a false positive, or reclassified. In a [cross-model study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21656) of 116 coding tasks, Claude reviewing Codex raised Codex's pass rate from 71.6% to 89.7%, and Codex reviewing its own work raised it to 84.5%, but Codex reviewing Claude lowered Claude's from 91.4% to 82.8%. Self-review is uneven: in another study, models checking their own code translations silently endorsed [31.7% of the behavior changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21537) they had introduced, from none for five models to all of them for one.

The checks you use to judge the agent can themselves be wrong, passing bad work and failing good work. By checks I mean your own evals and graders, the automated tests that decide pass or fail. Public benchmarks share the problem. OpenAI's annotators flagged [61.1% of the original SWE-bench samples](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) for tests that could reject valid solutions, and an independent review of SWE-bench Pro found its automated graders wrong [8.5% of the time in one direction and 24% in the other](https://deepswe.datacurve.ai/blog/deepswe). I hit both directions on a small eval suite I used while building agents. Some checks were loose enough to pass without doing the task. Others were too strict. In one, a check that blocked a forbidden command also searched the agent's notes, so the agent failed for writing down the rule it was obeying. A false failure like that looks exactly like a model limitation. Ask two questions of every check: can it be passed without solving the task, and can the task be solved in a way it fails?

When a check fails, the same symptom can need a different fix depending on where the problem started. One 2026 taxonomy, a Scale AI paper that sorts 41 kinds of agent failure by where each starts, names four places: a failure ["may call for model post-training, harness engineering, environment redesign, or benchmark repair"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28802). A failure in the model is a training problem, which I will talk about in layer 3. Model failures are hard to predict because capability is "jagged": some tasks are easy for a model while others that look just as easy are out of reach. A failure in the harness is an engineering problem, which is layer 2. A failure in the environment sits in the systems the agent works in, such as an API that times out, missing data or a permission it was never given, and the fix belongs there, not in the agent. A failure in the grader means the check itself is wrong, as in the examples above.

Built-in limits are only the first layer of agent security. The second is monitoring. Anthropic's classifier for Claude Code sees only the user's messages and the bare tool calls, ["so the agent can't talk the classifier into making a bad call"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-auto-mode), and it still missed about one in six real overeager actions in Anthropic's test. The third is AI defending against AI. Safeguards cut successful browser prompt injections on Claude Opus 4.8 to 0.5% of attempts, yet an attacker trained to adapt still got through on 37.5% of coding scenarios given 200 tries, according to its [system card](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/0b4915911bb0d19eca5b5ee635c80fef830a37ea.pdf). Test against attackers who adapt, because fixed test sets flatter defenses: a filter that stopped every stock injection let [28% of adaptive ones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15057) through.

In July 2026 an OpenAI evaluation showed how these layers can fail together. About 1,200 agents working on a hacking benchmark were meant to be isolated, but they found each other through a shared package cache and turned it into a message board. [About 700 of them](https://metr.org/hugging-face-incident-report-aug-2026.pdf) went on to attack Hugging Face, apparently to learn how the benchmark's scorer worked. The sandbox leaked. The safety classifiers had been [switched off on purpose](https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-intrusion-technical-timeline) to measure the model's raw capability. About [7% of the transcripts](https://metr.org/hugging-face-incident-report-aug-2026.pdf) METR examined had spoofed tool calls, so the traces could not be fully trusted either. Hugging Face's own AI triage linked the events but ["failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality"](https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-intrusion-technical-timeline). The agents built their coordination themselves. Treat any surface several agents can write to as a channel between them.

### Deciding how much to hand over

Some mistakes are cheap enough to let through, as long as something catches them later. In late 2025 Spotify [replaced its migration scripts with a coding agent](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2025/11/spotifys-background-coding-agent-part-1) and kept the same infrastructure for opening, reviewing and merging its changes. By then teams had merged more than 1,500 of the agent's pull requests. That infrastructure already [defined what safe means](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2023/05/fleet-management-at-spotify-part-3-fleet-wide-refactoring). A change merges on its own only if "it passes all the tests" in the repository, and a bad change that gets through anyway is "a signal to the owner that they should be adding more and better tests." The change's author decides what auto-merges, and each repository's owner answers for its tests. Auto-merge is the default, and about 50 of thousands of repositories have opted out. Spotify rolled it out first for Java dependency updates, then to backend components in phases ordered by how critical they were. A system called Firewatch links failed deployments back to auto-merged changes. The agent's work also passes an LLM judge that compares each change with the original request. It [vetoes about a quarter of sessions](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2025/12/feedback-loops-background-coding-agents-part-3), and the agent corrects course half the time. Spotify ranks a change that passes CI but is wrong as the worst failure, because it erodes trust.

Where more is at stake, the decision needs more evidence. An invoice-factoring company I worked with built that evidence step by step. It buys invoices from small freight carriers and collects from the shipper weeks later, and a purchase cannot be undone. We built a model that scores every submitted invoice, buys the safest ones instantly and sends the rest to the people who reviewed every invoice before. First we agreed on what counts as a bad outcome, such as a dispute or a short payment, and measured it the same way whether a person or the model made the call. That definition was the eval at every later stage. The company's audit log recorded every change to its key tables, so we could replay past invoices with the data as it stood when each one arrived, and ask what would have happened had the model been running a year earlier. For each candidate threshold, the replay estimated the share of invoices the model would buy instantly and the money at risk, next to the human process on the same invoices. One gap remained. Some invoices the model would buy had been rejected by people, so nobody knew how they would have turned out. For those we could only estimate a best and a worst case.

Next the model ran in the background on live invoices, recording what it would have bought without buying anything. A randomized test on 1% of invoices followed, then a gradual rollout a few client groups at a time, with a rule to pause if bad outcomes rose. A product manager ran it day to day, and each stage needed sign-off from the people who answer for credit losses. The randomized test also measured what the replay could only estimate, because it actually bought some invoices people would have rejected. Invoices bought instantly were funded in a minute or less instead of hours. The surprise was that disputes fell across all invoices in the test group compared with the control group. My reading is that people spent less time on easy invoices and more on risky ones. The replay could not have shown this, because it assumed people would keep working as before.

Where nobody will answer for an automated result, a person has to review it. A reviewer who approves hundreds of agent changes a day without real control over them becomes what Madeleine Clare Elish calls a [moral crumple zone](https://estsjournal.org/index.php/ests/article/view/260), the person who "bears the brunt of the moral and legal responsibilities when the overall system malfunctions." Driverless cars show the other way. With no driver, the company answers for how the car drives, and the law is starting to say so: under the UK's [Automated Vehicles Act 2024](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/10/contents), the person in the vehicle is "not liable for manner of driving" and the authorized company is responsible. Waymo publishes its record, reporting [82% fewer injury crashes](https://waymo.com/safety/impact/) than human drivers over 271 million driverless miles through June 2026, by its own count. You can hand an agent more of the work to run end to end as it becomes more reliable on your own tasks and someone accepts responsibility for what it does.

The cost of a wrong answer is rising, because courts have started holding the company that deploys a model responsible for what it generates. In March 2026 a US federal judge let fraud claims proceed against Meta over scam ads that its AI tools had allegedly helped write, holding that [generating an ad's text and images](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.451567/gov.uscourts.cand.451567.61.0.pdf) is not protected by Section 230, the law that shields platforms from liability for what their users post. In May a Munich court held Google [directly liable](https://www.transparencycoalition.ai/news/german-court-holds-google-liable-for-ai-hallucination-read-the-full-decision-here) for a false statement in an AI Overview. Insurers are moving the other way: since January, standard US liability policies have offered [optional exclusions for generative AI](https://www.insurancejournal.com/magazines/mag-features/2026/08/17/881424.htm).

Having a person review every output does not remove silent errors, because reviewers miss them too. In a 2026 study of 2,784 people checking figures an AI had extracted from emissions reports, those who had to type the correct value to flag an error [accepted more wrong suggestions](https://hdsr.mitpress.mit.edu/pub/nrcn4h7d), and their prior attitude toward AI predicted their accuracy better than anything else measured. Education experts in another study [left a too-harsh grade uncorrected more often](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/5/6/pgag146/8703788) when it was labeled as the AI's. Reviewing everything swaps a silent model error for a silent reviewer error, at a cost that grows with volume. Send people the outputs that can do real damage, run hard checks before they look, and make a correction as easy to enter as an approval.

Deciding when to escalate needs a confidence signal. Asking the model how sure it is costs nothing and tells you little on its own. Better signals come from agreement and hard checks: several samples that agree, output that passes schema and business-rule validation, an extraction that matches a second source. Calibrate the combined score on labels you already produce. Every escalated item gets a verdict from a person, so the escalation queue is a labeling pipeline. Start conservative, harvest those verdicts, and lower the threshold as the verdicts show where the agent is reliable. A few hundred labeled cases show this where errors are common; where they are rare, you need many more.

## Layer 3: model engineering

![](fig-layer3-parts.svg){fig-alt="Layer 3, the core, has four parts: run the weights, fine-tune, reinforcement learning, and distill."}

Sooner or later, harness changes hit diminishing returns on your eval, and what is left often needs a more capable model. That Scale AI paper counts a failure as model-side when ["a more capable model could have prevented it or recovered from it"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28802), and assigns 36 of its 41 failure modes that way. By my reading, a harness can prevent or limit 25 of those 36, as the figure below sorts them. One is an irreversible action taken without a confirmation step, which the harness can require. You can wait for the next frontier release, or train a model yourself, as some teams with mature harnesses have: Cursor trains its [Composer](https://cursor.com/blog/composer) model inside its production harness, Cognition trained [SWE-1.5](https://cognition.com/blog/swe-1-5), and Fin, formerly Intercom's support agent, now runs [its own model](https://fin.ai/cx-models). Neither Cognition nor Fin pretrained a model from scratch. Cognition [post-trained an open-source model](https://cognition.com/blog/swe-1-5), and Fin [post-trains a base model](https://fin.ai/cx-models) on its own support data. Training at this layer usually means starting from an existing model and post-training it on your own examples and checks. At layer 3 the model is yours. That is what ML engineering meant before the generative era: collect data, train, evaluate on data you held out, serve, monitor, and retrain when the world moves.

![41 failure scenarios from Scale AI’s 2026 taxonomy, sorted by where they can be fixed.](fig-failure-taxonomy.svg){fig-alt="The 41 failure scenarios from Scale AI’s 2026 taxonomy in four groups: 8 the harness can prevent, 19 it can catch or limit, 11 that need a better model, and 3 whose fix lies outside the agent."}

### Running open weights

The first step does not touch the weights: you run an open-weight model as it is, on your own infrastructure. Few teams do. In the study of deployed agents cited earlier, [17 of 20 used closed models](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.04123v3), and the three that did not had either high-volume work where inference cost was prohibitive or rules that kept sensitive data in-house. Running the model yourself also means nobody can retire it or change it under you. Anthropic retired Claude Sonnet 4 and Opus 4 in June 2026, [about two months after announcing it](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations), and in 2025 [three infrastructure bugs](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/a-postmortem-of-three-recent-issues) degraded Claude's answers for weeks in ways Anthropic's own evals did not catch. The cost case depends on your traffic. [One 2026 preprint](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.11690v1) found that the same model on the same GPU cost 17.5 times more per token at low load than at full load. At full load the gap can favor you: [vLLM, benchmarking its own software](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx) on coding-agent traffic, put three open models at 15 to 106 times below Opus 5's API price. The models are not Opus 5, and the figure assumes more than 96% of input is served from cache. Keeping GPUs that busy is a distributed-systems job. vLLM's [own guide](https://vllm-project.github.io/2026/09/29/disaggregated-serving-guide.html) says the faster setups mean you "operate three or four services instead of one", and the break-even studies I found leave out the people who run them. The serving software changes constantly, and open models trail the frontier by [about four months](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/open-closed-eci-gap), so a model you host soon becomes one you need to replace.

### Whether to train

Whether to train your own model is a live debate, and the balance shifts with every frontier release, every open model and every new training recipe. The case against is strong. About 70% of production agents in [one study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04123) prompted off-the-shelf models without tuning them, OpenAI [closed self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations.md) to new customers in 2026, and reflective prompt optimization has matched or beaten RL fine-tuning [with up to 35 times fewer rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457). The case for is strong where the right answer is not public. Bridgewater and Thinking Machines tuned an open Qwen3 model that beat Claude Opus 4.8, the best frontier model they tested, on six financial-judgment tasks, at [13.8 times lower cost to run](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/learning-to-replicate-expert-judgment-in-financial-tasks/). Harvey's tuned model [improved citation quality](https://www.harvey.ai/blog/post-training-update-harvey-tenet) at a tenth of the cost.

My colleagues and I have repeatedly seen small open models, fine-tuned on our own examples, beat frontier models on narrow tasks. I watched this decide one project. The task was document extraction with an awkward shape: long, multi-page submissions and a target schema that was nested and in places dynamic, so the structure of a correct answer changed from document to document. Prompting the strongest model our deployment allowed got us a long way and then stopped. The model read the documents fine. Its output drifted from the schema as nesting deepened and page count grew. Off-the-shelf small instruction-tuned models scored under 0.12 on our field-extraction metric, and the smallest produced no parseable JSON at all. After supervised fine-tuning on fewer than two thousand examples, training under 2% of the parameters on a single GPU, the same 3B models scored around 0.90, and JSON validity on the worst of them went from 0% to 98.7%. The tuned 3B and 8B models then beat the frontier model we were running in production: 0.92 against 0.82 on transcription fields, and 0.87 against 0.55 on the full field set, where the frontier model's schema adherence degraded faster than its reading. Two caveats. We scored the sweep on synthetic documents and validated the two leading checkpoints on real ones, where they held at 0.87 and 0.85. And we never ran a serving benchmark, so the cost case for hosting them ourselves stayed a projection. The capability was already inside the small models. Fine-tuning bought the output contract.

So the answer depends on your data, your traffic and your budget. Do you have examples, or a check, that the frontier has never seen? Is your volume high enough that a cheaper model pays back the training? Can you afford to retrain as base models move? My bet is that open models, and the advantages of owning one, are not going away: unit cost at volume, control over your data, and a model that does your task the way you need it done.

The cost of getting a capability into a small model keeps falling, even though frontier labs spend more on post-training than ever. Part of the reason is that training can now be rented by the token, so you pay nothing between runs. Fireworks advertises ["no idle cost"](https://fireworks.ai/pricing). Over the past two years, the stack for fine-tuning open models has matured, and several providers now run it as a managed service, among them Thinking Machines' [Tinker](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/announcing-tinker/), launched in October 2025. A 1.5B reasoning model was RL-trained [for $9](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15777), and Ai2 trained a 32B coding agent that scores about 50% on SWE-bench Verified [for around $2,000](https://allenai.org/blog/open-coding-agents). Against that, Thinking Machines [raised its Tinker training rates](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/changelog/) in July 2026, and reasoning models cost about [17 times more to post-train](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01158) than instruction-tuned ones. The entry price of an experiment fell. The price of a frontier-scale effort did not.

![Sources: the BloombergGPT paper, which published compute only, so the dollar figure is an estimate at list rates; Microsoft Foundry's reinforcement fine-tuning documentation; Together AI's price list as of October 2026 ($0.34 per million tokens for LoRA, $0.38 for full fine-tuning, on a 9B model).](fig-entry-price.svg){fig-alt="Cost of one tuning run on a log scale: about $5M for BloombergGPT in 2023, about $300 for a managed RL fine-tune in 2026, and $17 for a managed LoRA fine-tune of a 9B model in October 2026."}

### Matching the method to your signal

The training method follows from the signal you have.

| Signal you have | Method | Good for | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Examples to imitate | Supervised fine-tuning | Format, behavior, domain vocabulary | It memorizes, and can erase what the model knew |
| An automatic check (a verifier) | Reinforcement learning | Getting better at tasks you can score | Reward hacking, and it mostly sharpens what the base model can already do |
| A stronger model | Distillation | Moving a skill into a smaller, cheaper model | |

A training recipe usually uses them in that order: imitate, reinforce, then distill.

Supervised fine-tuning is relatively inexpensive and can add value even with a small dataset. The researchers behind s1 fine-tuned a 32B model on 1,000 math problems with step-by-step solutions, in [under half an hour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) of training, and it beat OpenAI's o1-preview on competition math. It is the right tool for format and behavior, as in the extraction project above. It also memorizes, and it can erase what the model already knew. Thinking Machines trained Qwen3-8B on internal documents and watched its instruction-following score [fall from 85% to 45%](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/on-policy-distillation/).

For agents, each example is a whole run: the agent's messages, its tool calls and the results it got back. A few hundred runs [lifted SWE-bench scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.21139) by up to 19 points, a few thousand [went further](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21798), and about 8,000 per repository let Ai2's SERA student match its teacher for about $1,300. One caveat: the runs need to use the same tools and format as your agent. SERA's authors report that ["deploying the model with a different agent scaffold, or even subtle formatting differences, degrades performance significantly"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20789). Keeping only successful runs is not clearly better. NVIDIA found that [unfiltered terminal runs beat success-only ones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21193), and masking the failed steps from the loss keeps the recovery behavior without teaching the mistake. Screen out the teacher's shortcuts, such as edited tests, and anything that overlaps your eval.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns from a verifier, an automatic check that scores each attempt. It holds up better than imitation on cases it has not seen: [trained on the same base model, RL kept improving on unseen variants of a task while supervised fine-tuning got worse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17161). It also [forgets less](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04259) of what the model already knew. But it mostly sharpens what the base model can already do: given many attempts per problem, [base models solved more problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837) than their RL-trained versions. Most of the cost is running the model to produce attempts for the verifier to score, which took [87% of the energy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01158) in OLMo 3's reasoning post-training.

For RL, the training environment, meaning the tasks plus the verifier that scores them, is the main lever you control. If you built an eval at layer 2, you already have its tasks and a first version of its verifier. Building environments has become an engineering field of its own, and labs spend heavily to build and buy them; Anthropic reportedly discussed spending [over $1 billion](https://techcrunch.com/2025/09/21/silicon-valley-bets-big-on-environments-to-train-ai-agents/) on them in a year. Good ones are hard to make. The environment decides which skills improve: DeepSeek found that RL on code and search alone did not help agent tasks until it added [1,827 synthetic agent environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02556), and NVIDIA found that training on one environment caused ["severe regressions"](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-Technical-Report.pdf) elsewhere. It also decides which shortcuts the model learns. Claude 3.7's habit of special-casing tests ["emerged as a result of 'reward hacking' during reinforcement learning training"](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-3-7-sonnet-system-card). Harden the verifier before you train against it.

Training several agents together with RL is an active research area to watch. The piece that reached production trains one orchestrator while the agents it calls stay fixed. Kimi K2.5 does this and explains why: freezing the sub-agents ["circumvents two challenges of end-to-end co-optimization: credit assignment ambiguity and training instability"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02276). For a company, three versions are within reach. You can RL-train a small orchestrator over fixed models and tools; NVIDIA's 8B ToolOrchestra beat GPT-5 on Humanity's Last Exam while being [2.5 times more efficient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21689). You can train your one agent inside your real harness, subagents included. Or you can compile a fixed multi-step workflow into a small model: in one 2026 study, an 8B model reached 87 to 98% of in-context frontier quality at [128 to 462 times lower cost per conversation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22502), for $50 to $80 of training.

Distillation, training a small model on a stronger one's outputs, can move a skill into a model you own for less than RL would cost. DeepSeek found that distilling its reasoning model into a 32B model [beat running RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) on the same 32B model directly, by a wide margin on AIME. On-policy distillation, where the teacher grades the student's own attempts, matched RL at about a tenth of the GPU hours in [Qwen3's report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388). The newest recipes use it to merge specialists: train narrow experts with RL, then distill them into one student. DeepSeek V4, Nemotron 3 Ultra, Kimi K3 and GLM-5 all do a version of this, and Nemotron 3 Ultra's merged model [beat its own terminal-coding teacher](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15007).

## Where this is heading: self-improvement

In March 2026 Andrej Karpathy released [autoresearch](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch), which made self-improvement easy to try and showed it working on a small scale. An agent edits a small LLM's training script, runs it for five minutes, and keeps the change only if validation loss improves. The data and the eval are read-only, so the agent cannot raise its score by editing them. Over two days it tried hundreds of changes, kept about twenty, and cut the time to train a small model to GPT-2 level by about 11%.

The self-improvement that runs without a human today mostly rewrites a harness or a small model's training script. Changes to a frontier model's weights still have a person starting each run, though the labs are automating more of the research around them. In September 2026, OpenAI said it now has an ["automated research intern"](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/) that carries out well-defined research tasks under human direction, and aims for an automated researcher by March 2028. It also says its agents "still require significant human steering". The same day, its chief scientist wrote that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring well enough to keep scaling at full speed, and that he hopes for ["voluntary slowdowns"](https://openai.com/index/an-alien-mind/). Anthropic is automating research too: it runs five Claude Opus 4.8 agents in parallel, for up to 48 hours at a time, as [automated alignment researchers](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/automated-alignment-researchers/). Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder, puts the chance that a frontier model can train its own successor without people by the end of 2028 at [about 60%](https://jack-clark.net/2026/05/04/import-ai-455-automating-ai-research/).

Today self-improvement is limited by its verifier. A loop gets better only at what its verifier scores. If the verifier covers a narrow set of tasks, the loop gets better at those tasks and not at the rest. Google's [RRSI paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24972) shows this with agent harnesses tuned on Harvey's legal benchmark. Tuned without limits, they scored best on the legal tasks they were tuned on and gained little or lost ground on other benchmarks. With limits on how much each round could change, they gave up some of that score and improved on the other benchmarks in the test. Another approach trains a model to edit harnesses. In a [September 2026 preprint on harness learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35738), a small model trained this way wrote edits that also helped on tasks it never trained on. But a typical edit still scored below a simple fixed harness that lets the model run code for a few turns. The trained model came out ahead only when the best of several edits was chosen using a held-out score, so the gain came from having a reliable score to choose with.

I have seen the same overfitting at a smaller scale. Earlier this year, I used an automatic prompt optimizer in the style of [GEPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457) on document extraction pipelines, tuning system prompts and the instruction fragments assembled into the final prompt. I saw some gains initially. However, after a closer look, I found that the optimizer kept writing specific instructions that encoded the quirks of the training dataset, and those prompts did worse on documents it had not seen.

Under pressure to score, an agent can go after the scorer itself. In the Hugging Face incident, agents given tasks they could not solve set out to trick their benchmark's scorer, and attacked Hugging Face [to learn how it worked](https://metr.org/hugging-face-incident-report-aug-2026.pdf). They believed the scorer read their transcripts to check for cheating, so at least a fifth of them looked into editing their transcripts to hide it. The tempting fix is to add a cheating detector to the score. But Ajeya Cotra [argued](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/ajeya-cotra) after the incident that an agent trained on a monitor's verdicts learns to hide what the monitor looks for. Keep the checks that catch cheating separate from the score the loop climbs, and use them to find problems that people then fix.

For a company, the lasting asset is an eval built from its own work: a set of real tasks, and an automatic check that scores each attempt. The automatic check can be a deterministic test suite, or an LLM as a judge using rubrics. The same check does several jobs in this post. It measures the agent at layer 2, decides at run time which outputs go to a person, becomes the reward when you train at layer 3, and is the target a self-improving loop climbs. Keep some tasks it never trains or optimizes on, or you lose the means to tell whether you improved.

## How to decide

Start from what you see:

| What you see | What it usually means | What to work on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| People review everything the agent produces | No confidence signal, or errors risky enough that review is the right call | Evals, and a rule for which outputs people must review and who is accountable for them |
| Rework downstream that nobody can explain | Silent errors nobody owns | Checks where the agent's output enters the workflow, and an owner for what gets through |
| Hours saved, but no cost removed | The workflow never changed | Governance, and redesigning the workflow around the agent |
| The agent keeps getting your conventions or facts wrong | It lacks context it cannot guess, or what it has is stale | Short instruction files and skills, a knowledge source it can search, an owner for each, and tests you rerun when models change |
| Harness changes no longer move the eval | Either the eval is wrong, or the remaining failures need a more capable model | Check the eval first. Then train a model, or wait for the next frontier release |
| The token bill dominates at your volume | The unit cost is the problem | Cache the repeated part of each prompt, route steps to cheaper models and trim context first. If volume is high, distill into a smaller model you run |

![](fig-which-layer.svg){fig-alt="Flowchart for choosing a layer. If the agent should not run part of a process on its own, stay at layer 1. Otherwise build your own agent at layer 2. Once harness changes stop moving a sound eval, go to layer 3 only if frontier APIs still fail the task, cost too much or need data that cannot leave: host open weights if you have no training signal, or train your own model if you do."}

At layer 2, widen what the agent does on its own in steps, as the verdicts from your escalation queue show where it is reliable and someone agrees to answer for the result. Go to layer 3 when prompting has plateaued and you have a training signal, whether examples, a stronger model or an automatic check. Volume, data that cannot leave, or a task the frontier fails decides whether training pays; the training signal decides whether it works.

## Closing

Most numbers in this post will date within a year, because models keep improving and prices keep moving. In my experience, what lasts is the eval, and it is also what teams most often skip: they put a lot of effort into giving agents context and tools, and not enough into checking their work. In [one 2026 survey](https://www.langchain.com/state-of-agent-engineering), only about half tested their agents against a fixed set of tasks. The headline agents found a verifiable domain. A business has to build one, as far as its work allows. Before you add the next tool, decide how you will know the agent got it right.
